feedback: If the learner thinks all joints move the same way, compare the hinge motion of the knee/elbow with a ball-and-socket joint's rotation.
Connect the wrapping ligaments to their stabilising job: they hold the bones together through the full range of motion.
activities.intendedInsight: A synovial joint is a genuinely three-dimensional structure: ligaments wrap it and surfaces meet and rotate in space, which a flat diagram foreshortens.
learnerActions: Rotate and flex a 3D model of a knee or elbow.
Observe how the cartilage surfaces meet, how ligaments wrap around the joint, and how the hinge moves in space.
Describe how the joint surfaces glide against each other as the bone rotates about the pivot.
activities.title: Explore the joint in three dimensions

feedback: If a learner sorts correctly but can't predict failure consequences, revisit the model's disable moments: cut tendon → no force transmitted, bone won't move; torn ligament → joint unstable/loose but still powered.
Watch for the distractor 'tendons and ligaments both join muscles to bones' — correct to tendon = muscle-to-bone, ligament = bone-to-bone.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means mapping each connector to its function AND predicting the consequence when it fails.
learnerActions: Categorise roles as tendon vs ligament (e.g. 'moves the bone' vs 'stabilises the joint', 'muscle-to-bone' vs 'bone-to-bone').
Match each joint part to its function (cartilage → cushions; synovial fluid → lubricates; ligament → stabilises; tendon → transmits force).
Put the force path in order: muscle → tendon → bone → movement.
Answer a two-tier failure-prediction prompt: which would stop a muscle moving a bone at all — a cut tendon or a torn ligament — and why?
activities.title: Sort, match and sequence to check understanding
